pr.title: Make new passwords with generate and add --generate
pr.head: 2e4ae12de3c0197a49d04b2db53c34fe3e71fc44

summary: multipass is a password manager: a command-line program that keeps secrets in one file, encrypted under a passphrase. Until now it could store a password but not make one, so every new password came from another app, a shell one-liner, or someone's head. This pull request adds two ways to make one.

• multipass generate prints a new password and stores nothing. It opens no store, so it never asks for the passphrase.
  • multipass add <name> --generate makes a password and stores it as the entry's secret without ever printing it. With --clip it also copies the password to the clipboard, so you can paste it into a site's form.

There are three kinds of password: random characters (20 by default, with uppercase, lowercase, digits, and symbols each present), memorable words from the EFF's large word list, and PINs. Every run prints the password's strength on stderr. Strength is the base-2 logarithm of how many passwords the options could have produced, each equally likely, such as 130.9 bits. Anything below 64 bits gets a warning.

The drawing code lives in src/crypto/generate.rs, under the repository's constant-time rule. That rule says code there must not branch on a secret or use one as a memory index, because either can leak through timing. This pull request amends AGENTS.md to allow one exception: the decision to draw again, which depends only on a value that is then thrown away.

This is the bottom code layer of a stack on the password-generation plan (#20, still a draft). --syllables (#24) and --rules (#25) sit above it, so either can be dropped if the owner answers the plan's open questions the other way.

cards.title: Terms used on this page
cards.html:
• Recipe: the kind of password and its settings. It holds no secret, so it can be printed and compared.
  • Rejection sampling: picking a number below n without bias by drawing again whenever the random value falls in the leftover range that would favor some numbers.
  • Lemire's method: a rejection-sampling technique that multiplies a 16-bit value by n. The high half of the product is the index, and the low half says whether to reject.
  • Masked read: reading table[i] by touching every entry and keeping only the match with a bit mask, so the memory accessed does not depend on i.
  • Acceptance: the share of uniformly drawn strings that meet every requirement, which is the chance that one draw is kept.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• One review, at 2e4ae12, requests changes on one point. The README still says every command asks for the passphrase, which generate does not.
  • The checks, the release build, an expect run of add --generate, and a byte-for-byte comparison of the word list with the EFF's file all passed.

groups.title: Drawing passwords
groups.kicker: The one module that turns random bytes into a password and measures its strength
intro: Every choice a password needs is "pick one of n": a character from an alphabet, a word from the list, a separator, or the word to capitalize. So one function, below, makes every such pick without bias, and one family of functions, pick and pick_word, reads the chosen entry by scanning the whole table with a mask.

When the options require character sets, such as "at least one digit", draw_chars draws the whole password again until every set appears. It does not force a digit into a random position, because that would make some passwords more likely than others and the strength figure would be wrong.

Strength comes from the recipe alone, so printing it reveals nothing about the password. For random characters it is length × log2(alphabet) plus log2 of the acceptance, which a small dynamic program computes over which requirements are met so far, the current run of equal characters, and the set the last character came from.

checks.text: Random bytes come from crypto::random::fill, which calls read_exact on /dev/urandom. A short read or an error becomes an Err that every caller passes up with ?, so nothing falls back to a weaker source. Tests feed a SHA-256 stream through password_from instead.

files.note: The recipe types, the unbiased index draw, the masked reads, the drawing of characters and words, and the strength calculation, with their tests.

checks.text: reduce rejects exactly 65536 mod n of the 65,536 values and maps every other value evenly. every_16_bit_value_maps_evenly feeds each value once for n of 10, 94, 2,000, and 7,776, and would fail on a plain v % n.
Beside the rejection in below, this is the one branch on secret data: a password that misses a required set is thrown away whole. AGENTS.md names it as the second exception to the constant-time rule.

Each word sits in a 10-byte slot (9 for the longest word, 1 for the separator). This loop moves each real byte to its rank among the real bytes with masks, so the padding goes without branching on any word's length.
The pinned digest matches the word column of the EFF's published eff_large_wordlist.txt, checked by downloading it and stripping the dice numbers.

files.note: The EFF's large word list, 7,776 words, one per line, with the dice numbers removed. Four words hold a hyphen: drop-down, felt-tip, t-shirt, and yo-yo.

groups.title: The commands and their options
groups.kicker: Turning command-line options into a recipe, and wiring generate and add --generate
intro: src/generator.rs sits outside src/crypto because it handles only public text: it checks the options, builds a recipe, and formats the strength line. It also turns a drawn buffer into a String, which the repository's rules allow outside src/crypto for secrets kept as text.

main.rs parses the options and builds the recipe before any store opens, so a bad option fails without asking for the passphrase. generate returns before it looks for a store at all. add --generate opens the store, draws the password, saves it through Store::save (a temporary file at mode 0600 renamed into place), and prints only the strength line.

files.note: The options as given, their checks and error messages, the recipe they build, and the strength line.

checks.text: The options this layer offers do not come near one in a million: four characters with one character left in each of uppercase, lowercase, and digits keep about 5 draws in 10,000. The guard is there for --rules in #25, whose run limits can.

files.note: The generate command, --generate and --clip on add, the password options in parse, and the usage text.

checks.text: generate needs no store: run with HOME and MULTIPASS_STORE unset, a release build printed a PIN and its strength.

An expect run against a temporary --store showed add x --generate printing only the strength line, and get x printing the 20-character password. A second add without --force was refused. A wrong passphrase stored nothing.

groups.title: Rules, README, and plan
groups.kicker: The constant-time exception, the user-facing docs, and the plan details the code settled
intro: AGENTS.md holds the rules agents follow in this repository. It now names the redraw decision as an exception to the constant-time rule and says the word list is pinned by its SHA-256. The README gains a section on making passwords and credits the EFF's word list under CC BY 4.0 International, the license EFF's copyright policy gives its original material.

The plan records what the code settled: Lemire's method in place of a plain threshold, the optional count after --words and --pin, the four hyphenated words, floating-point shares in place of 256-bit integers (128 characters from 94 needs about 840 bits), and the exact form of each test.

files.note: Adds the redraw exception to the constant-time rule, and the word list's pinned digest beside the test vectors.
A new "Make new passwords" section, --clip extended to the new commands, and the EFF credit.

checks.text: This line still says every command asks for the passphrase, but generate opens no store and never asks. Say that every command except generate asks, or say so in the "Make new passwords" section.
